extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers and skeptics (atheists/unbelievers), students of natural theology and religious apologetics
extracted.subtask_description: Natural-theology guidance for demonstrating God's existence from the observable world (watch/clock analogy) and for judging the Divine origin of scripture. Emphasises plain observation, experiments, and specific signs of design versus chance or occult causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know God by his works (plain and simple observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: God 'does for the most part convince Men by his Works after this plain and simple Manner, which is obvious to all,' not by artfully invented philosophical argumentations requiring refined judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer proofs drawn from observable works of nature rather than abstruse philosophic speculation; the Bible and Psalms endorse looking to creation (e.g., Rom. i.20, Psalm 104) as a method accessible even to the weakest minds. Anti-pattern: relying primarily on deep speculative hypotheses instead of obvious natural evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of observations and experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: An observation of things themselves, which can only be made by experiments, is required to know God by his works; hence the Latin term 'observations' is appropriate for discoveries by experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence should be empirical and derived from direct observation/experiment. Avoid basing proofs on feigned hypotheses or purely speculative causes. 'Not enquiring into the same' (i.e., failing to observe) is reckoned among causes of atheism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features of systems indicative of design (enumerated properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a system shows (1) many parts, (2) variety of parts, (3) parts ignorant of all and even of themselves, (4) each acting in particular manners, (5) always unchangeably observing the same rule, (6) acting on many occasions and times, (7) none able to impart such motion to itself, (8) cannot produce the effect unless they come together, (9) omission of few circumstances prevents the effect, (10) the effect is of great use or importance — then one is justified in inferring a wise and understanding Agent (designer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this list as a checklist for judging whether an observed natural phenomenon evidences design. Example: the watch/clock and its wheels, springs, glass, and key illustrate these points. Scoring note: presence of multiple items (especially interdependence and sensitivity to missing circumstances) strengthens the design inference. Anti-pattern: explaining such properties by 'mere chance' or by unintelligent laws without accounting for purposive arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation of parts to purpose and appropriate material choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that parts are made of materials chosen for their function (e.g., brass to prevent rust, steel for a spring, clear glass to view hands) and that elements are precisely adapted (square pin fitting square cavity, a key adapted to wind a spring) indicates contrivance for a purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an artifact or natural structure, look for material-functional fit and precise adaptations. These provide strong evidence for an Artificer/Designer. Anti-pattern: treating material choice and specific adaptations as accidental or irrelevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence and fragility of arrangement (functional integration)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the operation of a whole depends on many parts so that a defect or alternate arrangement would render the whole useless, this interdependence indicates deliberate construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether removing or altering a single element negates the function; high functional integration favors inference of design. Example: the watch whose wheels, spring, and key must be properly combined to show time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improbability of arising by mere chance or unintelligent necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: If the regularity, niceness of make, and purposive arrangement of parts cannot plausibly be ascribed to mere chance or to ignorant/unstudied 'laws of nature', then design is the preferable explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the observed structure to known artifacts: asking whether a reasonable person would attribute a complex machine found in a desert to chance. Anti-patterns to reject: explaining complex purposive systems solely by 'chance' or by anonymous, unintelligent necessities without accounting for directed arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy/corroboration via artificial imitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Using smaller artificial counterfeits (wooden horse moved by springs, wooden bird, gilded globe with orbiting balls) or human artifacts (mills, ships, stadthouse) to mirror natural complexity can corroborate the inference to design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If smaller, imperfect imitations of natural works still strongly suggest design, then the much greater order of natural objects strengthens the demonstration. Use analogies to make the argument clearer to doubters, including those less affected by direct natural examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematician/expert test: comprehension of part relations implies conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematician or competent expert who thoroughly comprehends the relation of all parts and the services they render will, upon reflection, be as strongly convinced that the object was made by workmen and architects as of any demonstrated mathematical proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeal to domain experts' judgement: if an expert, after tracing structure and function, declares chance implausible, their verdict is a strong mark of design. Use this as persuasive evidence when addressing skeptical specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for a book's Divine origin — natural-science knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: First: If a book frequently mentions certain qualities of natural things (albeit incidentally) 'after such a manner as none but an Eminent, Wise, and Experienced Naturalist could do,' this supports the claim of extraordinary authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether descriptions of nature in the text display depth, accuracy, and perspective beyond typical contemporary knowledge. Presence of such passages counts in favor of divinity or extraordinary source of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for a book's Divine origin — information unknown to contemporaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondly: if the book represents properties of natural things with clearest words which, at the time it was written, were not known to any living person (nor could be known for want of instruments), this is evidence it was written with more than humane wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check historical claims: does the text assert facts that were demonstrably unknown at its purported time of composition? Verified instances of such knowledge strengthen the claim of supernatural origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for a book's Divine origin — prediction and limits of human knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Thirdly: if the book expressly mentions the bounds and limits of human knowledge or predicts future events in ways that could only be verified by later generations, such fulfilled predictions indicate a Divine power behind the writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for clear, testable prognostications or statements delimiting future discoveries; corroborated fulfilment of such predictions is taken as a hallmark of divine origin. Scoring note: the more specific and later-verified the prediction, the stronger the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject occult causes, intelligible fatality, and ignorant laws as sufficient explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not substitute 'occult causes', unintelligible fatality, or ignorant laws of nature (i.e., forces without knowledge or direction) for the inference of design; these are inadequate to explain purposive contrivances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating explanations for complexity, treat appeals to mysterious or unnamed laws as weak; prefer explanations that account for purposiveness, adaptation, and the attributes listed in the design-features rubric. Anti-pattern: invoking 'occult causes' to avoid the design inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative scale: natural world surpasses greatest human works
rubrics_metrics.description: If the visible world displays more wisdom, power, goodness, and variety than the greatest human works, then the inference to a supremely wise, powerful, and good Maker is stronger than the inference for any human artificer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use magnitude and pervasiveness of natural order as an amplification of the design argument. Example guidance: compare a watch to the structure of the world — the latter is far greater, so the inference to a divine Maker is correspondingly stronger.
